title: I Could Negotiate Anything for the Company. I Could Not Ask for Myself.
author: Kelly Mackin
summary: Kelly Mackin recounts how, despite being a skilled negotiator on behalf of her company, she repeatedly failed to advocate for her own compensation out of gratitude and fear -- until a sponsor once corrected her pay unprompted, and later she had to test her worth on the open market to finally get paid fairly. She concludes that the correction rarely comes from someone else, and that naming your worth and being willing to walk away is the real job of career advancement.
points: Mackin describes accepting a small raise into her first executive role without countering, driven by gratitude and a feeling she had something to prove.
She could negotiate hard for the company but 'would go quiet' when the subject was her own compensation.
A sponsor once corrected her pay unprompted to send a message that her worth wasn't a discount for being younger -- but she learned this was the rare exception, not the rule.
Years later, an inadequate promotion offer led her to test the open market, receive a real offer roughly 50% better, and use it to negotiate rather than accept quietly.
Once she signaled she might leave, the organization suddenly mobilized to recognize her value -- illustrating that attention to worth often arrives only when someone is about to walk away.
She reframes 'no' in negotiation as simply 'the current answer,' not a final wall, drawing a comparison to how toddlers absorb 'no' without giving up.
The piece concludes that raises and recognition don't arrive because they're earned -- they arrive because you ask, and no one else is coming to advocate for you.
quotes: I did not counter. I did not ask what the role was worth. I had no idea what I was worth, and I was not sure I wanted to find out, because finding out might mean asking, and asking might risk the seat I could not believe I had been given.

I could sit across a table and negotiate hard for the company all day long. Millions of dollars, difficult counterparties, terms that mattered. I was good at it. And then the thing on the table would be my own worth, and I would go quiet.
He said he wanted to send a message, that it was not acceptable to pay me less simply because I had fewer years than the people around me.

Most people will never have someone walk into their compensation and fix it out of a sense of fairness. It happened to me once, and it was a gift, and it would have been a mistake to build the rest of my career expecting it to happen again.
It was as if the entire organization woke up at once and realized I might actually walk, and the moment I might walk was the exact moment my value became a problem worth solving.
The worst thing anyone can say to you in a negotiation is no. That is the whole risk. Not ruin. Not exile. No. And we spend our whole childhoods hearing no.
The sponsor is rare. The raise you deserve does not arrive because you earned it. It arrives because you asked for it.
So stop waiting to be recognized. Name your worth, say it without apology, and treat no as the opening move, not the final word.
Talent gets you into the room. Asking is how you get paid for it.
